lesson.title: Vector databases: the recall, memory and latency contract
lesson.short: Exact search · HNSW/IVF/PQ · GPU graphs · filtered top-k
lesson.timeMeaning: Suggested independent study minutes; not scheduled contact time
lesson.lead: Approximation is a choice about which candidates you can afford to miss. A vector database must also handle filters, versions, updates and access rules.
goals: Define exact top-k and ANN recall using the same metric and filter.
Compare graph traversal, inverted-file pruning and vector compression.
Design a recall-matched single-GPU experiment and explain multi-GPU limits.

sections.title: How to use this supplemental session
sections.html: This is an original supplemental study session aligned to the user-provided syllabus. It is not an Edinburgh lecture or a verified Canvas assignment. The Canvas reading list and instructor-specific assessment instructions were not accessible. Suggested activities, timings, templates and checks below are practice guidance, not official requirements.

sections.title: Start with exact semantics
sections.html:
Each object has an embedding vector x in D dimensions. A query vector q is compared with a declared distance or similarity measure: Euclidean distance, cosine distance or inner product similarity. For unit-normalized nonzero vectors, squared Euclidean distance is 2−2 times their inner product, so these rankings agree. Without normalization, they need not agree. Specify preprocessing, dtype and tie-breaking when making exact ground truth.

An exact top-k query returns the k best eligible objects under that definition. An approximate nearest-neighbor index saves work by exploring only part of the search space or estimating distances with compressed representations. Recall@k compares its returned IDs with exact top-k IDs: intersection size divided by k, when at least k eligible items exist. If fewer exist, state the denominator convention and report result count.

ANN recall measures retrieval against an embedding metric. It does not prove that an embedding captures relevance, that retrieved text is factual, or that a downstream answer is correct.

Key takeaway

Separate embedding relevance, nearest-neighbor recall and downstream task accuracy. They measure different failure modes.

sections.title: Three complementary design choices
sections.html:
• Graph search: navigate neighbor links toward the query. Search breadth trades distance computations and memory traffic for recall. Graph construction and updates also cost time and memory.
  • Inverted-file search (IVF): partition the vector space and inspect selected clusters. More probes generally inspect more candidates. Skew, boundary queries and distribution shifts can make the chosen partitioning poor.
  • Quantization: store an economical code and estimate distances, then optionally rerank a shortlist using original vectors. A smaller index can fit a faster memory tier, but lost precision can change ordering.

These choices can be combined. A graph can use compressed vectors; an IVF index can scan quantized codes. An exact GPU scan remains a useful baseline for small collections or large query batches. Do not assume ANN always wins after build time, host-device transfer and filtering are included.

A vector database adds persistence, IDs and metadata, deletes, access control, concurrency and a policy for embedding/model versions. Comparing two index kernels alone does not evaluate these database-level properties.

Primary sources: pgvector official repository documentation.

sections.title: Worked example: recall and filtering
sections.html:
Original example. Exact top-5 IDs are {A,B,C,D,E}; an ANN query returns {A,C,E,G,H}. Recall@5 is 3/5=0.6. If a tenant filter makes only {B,D,F,G,H} eligible, the ground truth must be recomputed inside that subset. Comparing filtered output against the unfiltered top-5 is invalid.

Suppose an index retrieves 100 candidates and a filter independently accepts one percent of candidates. The expected survivor count is 1, not 10. Oversampling to 1,000 candidates gives an expectation of 10 survivors under this independence assumption, not a guarantee. Metadata can correlate with geometry; a different filtered-search strategy, iterative expansion or exact scan of the filtered subset may be necessary.

Access control must still be enforced before results or protected payloads are exposed. Approximation does not authorize cross-tenant data leakage. For deletes and embedding updates, state the freshness/snapshot rule and test that stale IDs cannot be returned improperly.

Exercise: after applying a filter, your index returns three IDs and all three are in the exact filtered top-10. Is recall 100%?

Worked answer. No. If ten eligible ground-truth neighbors exist, recall@10 is 3/10=0.3. Precision among the returned IDs may be 1.0. Returning too few neighbors is a distinct failure that recall should expose.

sections.title: Read two recent approaches
sections.html:
CAGRA (ICDE 2024) co-designs proximity-graph construction and search for GPU parallelism. Its evaluation includes batch-size effects and comparisons at stated recall levels. Treat its reported gains as measurements under the authors’ datasets, baselines and hardware; this session does not predict those gains on an H100. The author manuscript explicitly records acceptance.

RaBitQ (SIGMOD 2024) uses randomized quantization and a distance estimator with a theoretical error bound. Its binary code uses one bit per dimension, with additional information needed by the representation and surrounding index. A bound on distance estimation is not an unconditional exact-top-k guarantee: candidate selection and near-tied distances still matter.

Read the papers together: one emphasizes parallel graph execution; the other emphasizes compact representation and error analysis. Ask whether your bottleneck is traversal, memory capacity, bandwidth, build cost or distance arithmetic before selecting a mechanism.

sections.title: H100-sized mini-experiment: one GPU first
sections.html:
Inferred feasibility, not a reported result. Start with 1,000,000 vectors of dimension 768 and a separate held-out query set. FP32 vectors alone require 1,000,000×768×4=3.072 GB (decimal). A fixed degree-64 graph with 32-bit neighbor IDs adds 0.256 GB, giving a 3.328 GB lower-level estimate before build workspace, duplicated inputs, query buffers, allocator overhead and library-specific metadata. Check actual free device memory and the selected build path; do not infer peak allocation from this estimate.

On one available H100, compare an exact GPU scan, IVF-Flat or IVF-PQ, and CAGRA using a pinned supported library version. Sweep query batch size (for example 1, 32, 256), search effort and index parameters. Record recall@10 at matched operating points, p50/p95/p99 latency, QPS at stated concurrency, build time, peak device memory and host-device transfer. Separate kernel-only and end-to-end measurements. Warm up and synchronize before timing asynchronous GPU work.

Two H100s enable a separate optional sharding test. Search disjoint shards and globally merge candidates using the same metric. Exact local top-k from every shard suffices for global exact top-k, subject to ties. Approximate local top-k retains no such exactness guarantee. Measure routing, replication/partition strategy, cross-device transfer and merge overhead rather than assuming 2× speedup.

Primary sources: NVIDIA cuVS: CAGRA guide; NVIDIA cuVS: Benchmarking methodologies; NVIDIA cuVS: Installation.

sections.title: Exercises, failure cases and takeaways
sections.html:
Before accepting a benchmark, ask whether the query set was used for tuning, whether distance/preprocessing match, whether the exact baseline is correct and whether filters or updates change the conclusion.

Exercise: compare A at 20,000 QPS and 0.80 recall with B at 12,000 QPS and 0.96 recall. Which is faster at equal quality?

Worked answer. The data do not answer that question. Sweep each method’s parameters and compare at a shared recall target or show the quality/latency Pareto frontier. A is faster at its reported setting, but its quality is lower.

Exercise: can a one-bit code make an entire vector database 32 times smaller than FP32?

Worked answer. Not necessarily. The raw coordinate payload changes from 32 bits to one bit per dimension, but scale factors, centroids, graph links, IDs, original reranking vectors and metadata add storage. Report measured total and a breakdown.

Key takeaway

An honest ANN result reports recall, workload, batch size, latency/throughput, build cost and memory together.

quiz.question: The exact top-10 and returned top-10 share eight IDs. What is recall@10?
options: It cannot be computed without distance values.
quiz.explanation: Recall over IDs is intersection size divided by k when the exact eligible result has k elements.

questions.question: An ANN result returns three correct neighbors when ten eligible exact neighbors exist. What is recall@10?
questions.explanation: Recall@10 counts all ten required ground-truth neighbors in the denominator, even if the system returns fewer results.

questions.question: Which comparison isolates ANN speed at similar quality?
options: A parameter sweep followed by comparison at matched recall.
Highest QPS from each method regardless of recall.
A comparison with different distance metrics.
The smallest index without checking returned IDs.
questions.explanation: Quality changes with search effort and index settings. Comparing a shared recall operating point avoids confusing lower quality with faster execution.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: What is the FP32 coordinate payload for 1,000,000 vectors with 768 dimensions, in decimal GB?
questions.explanation: Each coordinate uses four bytes: 1,000,000×768×4 = 3,072,000,000 bytes. Index links and workspaces are additional.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: When do cosine and squared Euclidean rankings agree through the identity 2−2·dot-product?
options: Only when approximate search is disabled.
Only for vectors with negative coordinates.
For all arbitrary vectors without preprocessing.
questions.explanation: Unit normalization makes squared Euclidean distance 2−2 times the dot product. Without it, vector norms can change rankings.
